title: Replace, don't just remove
header_line: My analysis of one book on habits. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: Do you stop a bad habit, or give its energy a new place?
A student asked: negative habits are hard to just stop, for example getting a text while working and wasting five minutes on the phone. Do you cut them out or replace them?
I said I like replacing them: when you have energy in one direction, keep going with the energy, but channel it somewhere else. Recognizing what is triggering it is key.
I said I play classical music as a trigger to be productive and to sit at my desk, not listen to the phone. Pick something powerful that insulates you from negative triggers.

A student described it as a pathway: work is anchored to stress, stress is anchored to picking up the phone, and picking up the phone is anchored to relief. The more you use a pathway the deeper it gets.

The student said: with awareness of the pathway and the discipline to replace the trigger with something productive, repetition replaces the pathway until, when stress comes, the impulse is to meditate.
Another said: you just change the dopamine source. A student noted that the book goes into cue, craving and response later.
What is the trigger for the habit you want to replace, and what is the new response?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write one habit you want to replace.
Write what you feel after it.
Write a new response that gives the same relief.
Write what you will do the first time the trigger fires.

check.q: What did I prefer to do with a negative habit?
What did I say is key?
What did I use as a trigger to be productive?

recap: Find the trigger. Replace the response. Repeat.
